title: Moscow braces for the blow
pull: The mud froze, and the panzers came again

facts.text: Operation Typhoon, the German drive on Moscow, had stalled in the autumn mud. When frost hardened the ground in mid November 1941, Army Group Centre attacked again.

On the morning of 15 November the German Ninth Army struck first, south of Kalinin. A day later the 3rd and 4th Panzer Groups joined in, aiming to swing north of Moscow through Klin and Solnechnogorsk.
In the south, Guderian's Second Panzer Army began its drive below Tula on 18 November.

The city's defense rested with General Georgy Zhukov's Western Front. In the first half of November it received about 100,000 men, 300 tanks and 2,000 guns, and workers from Moscow and nearby towns formed 12 militia divisions.

Rokossovsky's 16th Army held the road through Volokolamsk and gave ground slowly. A counterattack there that Stalin had insisted on, against Zhukov's advice, ran straight into the German attack and collapsed.

Moscow had been under a state of siege since 20 October. Hundreds of thousands of Muscovites, most of them women, dug antitank ditches and trenches around the city. Estimates run from 250,000 to 600,000 people.
On 7 November Stalin had held the Revolution Day parade on Red Square anyway. The troops marched past the Kremlin and went straight on to the front.

On 19 November Stalin asked Zhukov: "Are you sure we will be able to hold Moscow? It hurts me to ask you that. Answer me truthfully as a communist." Zhukov said Moscow would be held, but that he needed reserves.
Klin fell on 23 November. By 28 November German tanks had a bridgehead across the Moscow Volga Canal at Yakhroma, and another spearhead was near Krasnaya Polyana, less than 20 miles from the Kremlin.
Zhukov's fresh reserve armies held, and the German attack ran out of strength in deep cold. In early December the Red Army struck back and drove the Germans away from the capital.

photoNote: Frame from the Soviet documentary film Na zashchitu rodnoy Moskvy (In Defense of Native Moscow), Central Studio for Documentary Film, December 1941: Moscow men in winter coats beside a newly built armored train. Commons tags it PD-Russia-1996 (public domain in Russia and, by the URAA date, in the US). Only 960 x 715 (Commons original 1020 x 762; the original download hit Wikimedia 429s, so this is the 960 px thumb). Weak lead: low resolution and not a famous image. Better looking but license doubtful alternative: civilians building a sandbag barricade on Smolenskaya Street, Moscow, 2 October 1941, by Leonid Dorensky (TASS), 3127 px, https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/File:Строительство_баррикады_на_Смоленской_улице_в_Москве.jpg , tagged only plain PD-Russia (photographer's death date not found), so I did not use it. NARA searches for US wartime copies of Soviet Moscow 1941 photos found nothing usable (the 208 AA Sovfoto copies are marked Restricted Possibly).
photoCredit: Moscow workers beside a newly built armored train, December 1941. Frame from the Soviet documentary In Defense of Native Moscow, Central Studio for Documentary Film, public domain.

declassified.fact: The famous story of Panfilov's 28, guardsmen said to have died stopping German tanks near Volokolamsk on 16 November 1941, was largely invented. A 1948 investigation by the Soviet chief military prosecutor traced it to articles in the army newspaper Krasnaya Zvezda, and Russia's State Archive published that report in 2015. Hard fighting did take place there that day.

kit.filmCaption:
Soviet film of the defense of Moscow, autumn 1941: a T-34 charging through the snow, a heavy gun firing from a forest position, ski troops in white, and light tanks moving up.

The shots come from the 1942 Soviet documentary Defeat of the German Armies near Moscow, released in America as Moscow Strikes Back. They are not dated to 15 November, the day the German drive on the capital began again, but they show the army that stood in its way.
kit.youtubeTitle: The Red Army Defends Moscow: Soviet Film, 1941 #shorts
kit.youtubeDescription:
Operation Typhoon, the German drive on Moscow, had stalled in the autumn mud. When frost hardened the ground in mid November 1941, Army Group Centre attacked again: on the morning of 15 November the German Ninth Army struck south of Kalinin, and the next day two panzer groups joined in north of the city. Moscow had been under a state of siege since 20 October, and hundreds of thousands of Muscovites, most of them women, dug antitank ditches around it. General Georgy Zhukov's Western Front received about 100,000 men, 300 tanks and 2,000 guns in the first half of November. On 19 November Stalin asked Zhukov whether Moscow could be held; Zhukov said it would be, but that he needed reserves. German tanks came within 20 miles of the Kremlin before the attack ran out of strength in deep cold, and in early December the Red Army struck back.

This is Soviet film of the defense of Moscow in the autumn and winter of 1941, from the documentary Defeat of the German Armies near Moscow (1942). The shots are not dated to 15 November. The film carries narration and music, so this clip runs silent.

Film: Defeat of the German Armies near Moscow (Central Studio of Documentary Film, 1942), via Wikimedia Commons, public domain.

kit_b.filmCaption:
Bayonets fixed, Soviet riflemen run across open snow. Then a cavalry squadron gallops over a frozen field, and more infantry push forward.

Soviet cameramen shot these scenes during the battle for Moscow in 1941. The film gives no day, so read them as that autumn and winter's fighting, not 15 November itself. The original carries narration and music, so this cut runs silent.
kit_b.youtubeTitle: Cavalry and Bayonets in the Snow at Moscow, 1941 #shorts
kit_b.youtubeDescription:
In mid November 1941, with the autumn mud frozen hard, the German army renewed its drive on Moscow. The Ninth Army attacked south of Kalinin on 15 November, two panzer groups followed the next day, and Guderian struck below Tula on the 18th. Rokossovsky's 16th Army gave ground slowly on the Volokolamsk road while Muscovites, most of them women, dug ditches and trenches around the capital. Klin fell on 23 November, and by the 28th German spearheads stood less than 20 miles from the Kremlin. Then the attack ran out of strength in deep cold, and in early December the Red Army struck back.

This film shows Soviet riflemen charging with bayonets, a cavalry charge across the snow, and infantry advancing, from a 1942 Soviet documentary of the battle. The shots are not dated to 15 November. The film's narration and score are left off, so the clip is silent.
